DOCKER CACHE ORDER CHECK · RUNS IN YOUR BROWSER

Is your Dockerfile busting its own build cache?

Paste a Dockerfile and see whether its instruction order defeats Docker's own layer cache: a dependency manifest copied and installed after the whole build context, an install command with no isolated manifest copy at all, and an apt-get update run without install in the same layer — the exact anti-patterns Docker's own "Leverage build cache" documentation names and gives the fix for.

Nothing is uploaded. Everything runs in this browser against the text you paste in.

Check a Dockerfile

    Prefer a CLI, or want this in CI before a merge?

    Same logic, zero dependencies, one file:

    node cli.mjs                       # scan every Dockerfile under .
node cli.mjs /path/to/repo         # scan a specific checkout
node cli.mjs --format json
node cli.mjs --fail-on-risk        # exit 2 if any finding exists

    Get cli.mjs — Node 18+, nothing to install, no network call ever. --fail-on-risk makes it a one-line CI gate on any Dockerfile change.

    What's checked

    CheckHow
    Manifest copied/installed after a broad copyA dependency manifest (package.json, requirements.txt, go.mod, Gemfile, composer.json, Cargo.toml, ...) is copied and its install command runs, but only after a whole-build-context COPY . . already ran earlier in the same build stage
    Install with no isolated manifest copyAn install command (npm ci, pip install -r requirements.txt, ...) runs with no earlier instruction naming its manifest file specifically — only a broad copy ever reaches it, so there is no dependency layer to cache at all regardless of order
    apt update/install split across layersA RUN instruction runs apt-get update (or apt update) without also running install/upgrade/dist-upgrade in that same instruction — Docker's own Dockerfile best practices name this exact split as the cause of a stale, separately-cached package index

    Checked ecosystems: npm/yarn/pnpm, pip, Go modules, Bundler, Composer, and Cargo. Each build stage (every section between FROM lines) is checked independently, and COPY --from=<stage> is never treated as a broad context copy, since it copies another stage's output rather than your source tree. See why this happens, and this checker's own named limits, or how this compares to reviewing a Dockerfile by eye.

    Common questions

    Why does putting COPY . . before installing dependencies break the Docker build cache?

    Docker caches each instruction's layer and only re-runs an instruction (and everything after it) when its own inputs change. If COPY . . runs before the dependency install step, that COPY layer's cache key includes every file in your source tree — so any source change at all, even a one-line comment, invalidates it and every layer after it, including the install. Copying just the manifest file (package.json, requirements.txt, go.mod) and running the install before copying the rest of the source means the install layer's cache key only changes when the manifest itself changes.

    Why does apt-get update need to be in the same RUN as apt-get install?

    Docker's own Dockerfile best practices documentation states this directly: a RUN apt-get update by itself is cached as its own layer, and Docker will reuse that cached layer on a later build even though the actual package index it downloaded is now stale. If a later, separately cached RUN apt-get install then runs against that stale cached update, it can resolve versions the package index no longer serves and fail, or silently install older packages than a fresh update would have found.

    What if my Dockerfile never copies a manifest file at all?

    Then there is no dependency layer to cache in the first place: the only route by which the manifest reaches the image is a broad copy, so any changed file in the build context invalidates the install regardless of instruction order. This checker reports that case separately ("install with no isolated manifest copy") because the fix is different — add a COPY that names the manifest file specifically, before the broad copy, not just reorder existing instructions.

    Is anything uploaded?

    No. Everything is computed in your browser from the Dockerfile text you paste in, and nothing you type is sent anywhere. The CLI makes no network call either — it only reads files already on your own disk.

    No warranty. This tool is provided free and as-is, without warranty of any kind, express or implied. It is not engineering advice, and it does not replace actually building the image and measuring your cache hit rate. It reports whether an instruction order matches one of three documented cache-busting patterns — nothing more, and it does not know whether a flagged pattern was deliberate in your case (some multi-stage builds intentionally copy broadly in a stage that is never cache-sensitive). You are responsible for reviewing and verifying its output before relying on it. To the maximum extent permitted by law, the authors accept no liability for any loss or damage arising from its use.

    Best-effort hosting, no SLA. These tools are free, experimental, and may be slow, broken, moved, or taken offline without notice. We do not promise uptime, backups of anything you type, or that a URL will keep working. Do not use this as a system of record. If a tool needs to survive, get cli.mjs and run it yourself.

    Everything runs in your browser. Nothing you type is ever uploaded; there are no accounts, cookies, or analytics vendors. Anonymous feature events (dockerfile_checked, example_loaded) are counted only in local storage and can be deleted with the button below. Do Not Track and Global Privacy Control are honoured.

    Also worth a pass on the same repo: Docker Base Image Pin Check checks whether your FROM lines are pinned to a content digest, and Docker Build Secrets Check checks for a secret leaking into the build context or an image layer — the same read-only, no-upload, zero-dependency shape applied to two different failure classes in the same file.

    Free and open source. If this saved you a slow rebuild, the code is under an MIT licence — support is entirely optional and never changes what the tool does.

vs-manually-reviewing-a-dockerfile.html.text:
← back to the checker

This checker vs. reviewing a Dockerfile by eye

The usual way to catch a cache-busting Dockerfile is to read it top to bottom during code review and notice anything that looks wrong. That works well for the textbook case — a five-line Dockerfile with COPY . . sitting right above RUN npm ci. It works much less well the moment catching the mistake requires tracking state across the whole file: which manifest was copied where, whether an install command ever got an isolated copy at all, or whether a later instruction silently depends on an earlier one several lines up.

What each one is for

Reviewing a Dockerfile by eye is free and needs no tool: read it start to finish and flag anything that looks off. It works well on short, single-stage Dockerfiles where the mistake is right next to its cause.

This checker tracks, per build stage, every manifest copy and every install command it has seen so far and reports exactly which instruction pairs violate the ordering — the bookkeeping a read-through has to do silently, in your head, across however many lines and stages the file has.

QuestionWhere to answer it
Is a COPY . . sitting right above the install command, in an otherwise short Dockerfile?Either one. A read-through catches this at a glance, and so does this checker.
Was the manifest ever copied on its own, anywhere in the file, or only ever inside a broad copy?This checker. Answering this by eye means cross-referencing every COPY's source list against every install command's ecosystem across the whole file.
Does a later RUN apt-get install quietly rely on an earlier, separately-cached apt-get update?This checker. Neither line looks wrong read on its own — the split is only visible across the two.
Does a broad copy in an unrelated build stage matter here?This checker, which resets its state at every FROM. By eye, "there's a COPY . . somewhere in this file" can read as a red flag regardless of which stage it is actually in.
Is anything I enter uploaded anywhere?Neither. A read-through involves no tool at all, and this checker runs entirely in your browser.

Common questions

Isn't a bad COPY . . before npm install obvious just from reading the file?

When the whole Dockerfile is five lines and the COPY . . is right above the install, yes. It stops being obvious the moment the file has multiple stages, several COPY instructions for different purposes, or the manifest copy and the broad copy are separated by other instructions — catching it by eye then means tracking, in your head, which lines named which files and in what order, across the whole file, which is exactly the kind of bookkeeping a deterministic scan does better than a read-through.

What does reading the Dockerfile not tell you at all?

Two things this checker reports that a read-through has no natural way to surface. First, whether an install command ever has an isolated manifest COPY anywhere in the file, as opposed to only ever seeing the manifest bundled inside a broad copy — that requires tracking every COPY's sources against every install command's ecosystem, not just scanning for an obviously misplaced line. Second, whether a RUN apt-get update earlier in the file is the only update backing a RUN apt-get install several lines later — a split that looks completely ordinary read top to bottom, because nothing about either line looks wrong in isolation.

Does multi-stage build syntax make this harder to review by eye?

Yes, more than it first appears. Each FROM starts a fresh build stage with its own cache lineage, so a broad copy in an earlier stage that is never cache-sensitive (a throwaway builder stage, say) says nothing about a later stage's own instruction order — but by eye, seeing COPY . . anywhere in the file can read as a red flag regardless of which stage it is in. This checker resets its state at every FROM for exactly that reason.

Is anything I paste into either process uploaded?

There is nothing to upload either way — reviewing a file by eye involves no tool at all, and this checker runs entirely in your browser against the text you paste in. The CLI makes no network call either; it only reads files already on your own disk.

No warranty. This page and the linked checker are provided free and as-is, without warranty of any kind, express or implied. They are not engineering advice, and they do not replace actually building the image and measuring your cache hit rate. You are responsible for reviewing and verifying the output before relying on it. To the maximum extent permitted by law, the authors accept no liability for any loss or damage arising from its use.

This page names no specific product. "Reviewing a Dockerfile by eye" describes a manual habit every developer already has access to, not any company's product or service.

Nothing leaves your browser. The checker this page links to runs entirely client-side; nothing you enter is uploaded anywhere.

why-docker-build-cache-gets-busted.html.text:
← Back to Docker Cache Order Check

Why Docker build cache gets busted

Docker builds an image layer by layer, one per instruction, and caches each layer keyed on that instruction and everything that fed it. On a later build, the moment one layer's cache key changes, that layer and every layer after it re-run from scratch — caching is not per-instruction independent, it is a chain that breaks at the first change and stays broken for the rest of the build. All three checks here are different ways of breaking that chain earlier than necessary.

Mistake 1: copying the whole build context before installing dependencies

A very common Dockerfile shape:

FROM node:20
WORKDIR /app
COPY . .
RUN npm ci

COPY . .'s cache key is derived from every file in your build context. Change one line of application source — not a dependency — and that COPY layer's key changes, which invalidates it and the RUN npm ci layer after it, so dependencies reinstall on every single build regardless of whether package.json actually changed. Docker's own "Leverage build cache" documentation gives the fix directly: copy the manifest alone first, install, then copy the rest of the source:

FROM node:20
WORKDIR /app
COPY package.json package-lock.json ./
RUN npm ci
COPY . .

Now RUN npm ci's cache key depends only on the two files named in the COPY immediately before it. A source-only change invalidates the final COPY . . but reuses the cached install layer untouched.

Mistake 2: an install with no isolated manifest copy at all

Sometimes there is no separate manifest COPY to reorder — the manifest only ever reaches the image via a broad copy:

FROM python:3.12
COPY . .
RUN pip install -r requirements.txt

Reordering these two lines does not fix anything, because there is no instruction whose cache key depends on requirements.txt alone — COPY . .'s key depends on the entire tree either way. The fix is to add a manifest-only copy, not just move existing lines:

FROM python:3.12
COPY requirements.txt .
RUN pip install -r requirements.txt
COPY . .

Mistake 3: apt-get update in its own layer

Docker's own Dockerfile best practices documentation names this one directly. Splitting the package index refresh from the install:

RUN apt-get update
RUN apt-get install -y curl

caches the update as its own layer. On a later build where nothing above it changed, Docker reuses that cached layer rather than re-running apt-get update — so the install step can resolve package versions against an index that is now stale, weeks or months old, even though the RUN apt-get install line itself looks unchanged. Combining them in one instruction means the index is always as fresh as the layer that installs against it:

RUN apt-get update && apt-get install -y curl \
    && rm -rf /var/lib/apt/lists/*

What this tool checks, and what it deliberately doesn't

CheckSourceOut of scope for v0
Manifest copy/install after a broad copyText/regex scan of COPY/ADD and RUN instruction order, per build stageWhether the broad copy was actually necessary before the manifest copy for some other reason specific to your build — this tool reports the pattern, not your intent
Install with no isolated manifest copySame scan, checking whether any earlier COPY/ADD names the ecosystem's manifest file specificallyManifests split across multiple non-standard file names this tool's ecosystem list does not recognize
apt update/install splitText match for apt-get update/apt update and install/upgrade/dist-upgrade within the same RUNOther package managers' equivalent split (apk update/apk add, yum makecache/yum install) — not checked in v0

Wiring it into CI before a merge

Check a changed Dockerfile before it merges:

- name: Check Dockerfile cache order
  run: node ventures/docker-cache-order-check/cli.mjs --fail-on-risk

Exits 2 when any of the three patterns is found, so a Dockerfile change that would reinstall dependencies on every build is caught in the same review that introduces it.

Common questions

Isn't this just what hadolint or a Dockerfile linter already does?

A per-line Dockerfile linter (hadolint and similar tools) checks each instruction in isolation against a rule — pin this FROM tag, add --no-install-recommends here. As far as this project could determine from hadolint's own published rule index, none of its rules reason about the relative order of two different instructions across a Dockerfile, which is what all three checks here do: they only make sense read as a sequence (was the manifest copied before or after the broad copy; did the same RUN combine update and install).

Does BuildKit already fix this automatically with its own caching improvements?

No. BuildKit changed how layers are cached and introduced cache mounts (RUN --mount=type=cache) for a package manager's own download cache, which is a genuinely different, complementary optimization. It does not reorder your instructions or infer that a COPY . . before an install was a mistake — the Dockerfile's instruction order is still exactly what you wrote, and BuildKit still invalidates a layer whenever an earlier layer's cache key changes, which is the mechanism this checker's three patterns each defeat.

Will this tell me whether my build cache is actually being reused?

No, and it does not try to. Measuring actual cache hit rate requires running real builds and reading BuildKit's own build output. This tool is a static check of the Dockerfile text: it reports an instruction order that is a documented cause of cache invalidation, before you have run a single build, so you can fix it in review instead of noticing it from a slow CI pipeline.

No warranty. This page and the tool it documents report whether a Dockerfile's instruction order matches one of three documented cache-busting patterns — nothing more. It is not engineering advice and does not know whether a flagged pattern was deliberate in your case. Verify against your own build's measured cache behavior before relying on it. Back to the tool.
